text:
<meta>This page continues the discussion on assessing human character through "nine tests" and contrasts the humility of the sage with the arrogance of the common man.</meta>

Employ them with wine to observe their standards; mix them in social gatherings to observe their demeanor <note>literally: color or facial expression</note>. Through these nine tests, even the most unworthy person can be identified.

Zheng Kaofu <gloss>styled Fu</gloss>
<margin>A member of the ducal house of the State of Song and the tenth-generation ancestor of Confucius</margin>
received his first commission <note>the rank of Officer</note> and walked with a slight stoop;
<margin>Officer</margin>
<margin>A bent back</margin>
he received his second commission <note>the rank of Great Officer</note> and walked with a deep hunch;
<margin>Great Officer</margin>
<margin>Bending the body low, not daring to obstruct the path</margin>
he received his third commission and walked with a profound bow, scurrying along the walls <note>out of modesty</note>.
<margin>Kaofu's humility was like this</margin>
Who would dare not to take him as a model? 
<margin>Who would dare not take him as a law?</margin>

But as for common men:
<margin>Ordinary men</margin>
upon their first <unclear>commission</unclear>, they become boastful and grand;
<margin>A look of pride and arrogance</margin>
upon their second commission, they dance atop their carriages;
<margin>Riding in a carriage and dancing with elation</margin>
upon their third commission, they address their elders by their personal names <unclear>one character, ink blot</unclear>.
<margin>Calling paternal uncles by their names</margin>

How different was the yielding virtue of Xu You of old!
<margin>How great was the yielding virtue of Xu You in the past!</margin>
There is no greater thief than a virtue possessed of intention; if the heart has intention, the heart has eyes <gloss>contact</gloss>.
<margin>To have a heart set on virtue is the thief of virtue</margin>
<margin>When the heart is enslaved by the appearance of things, virtue becomes increasingly perverse</margin>
Once there is this outward cleverness, one practices "inner vision," and through inner vision, one is ruined.
<margin>From this, looking back into the heart, there is constant turmoil, and one can never complete virtue or advance in the Dao</margin>
There are five "ominous virtues," and the central virtue <note>referring to the mind or heart</note> is the chief among them.
<margin>The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and mind</margin>
<margin>The mind/heart</margin>

<summary>The text contrasts the growing humility of the official Zheng Kaofu with the increasing arrogance of commoners as they rise in rank. It warns that intentional or self-conscious virtue acts as a "thief" that destroys true spiritual progress.</summary>
<keywords>Zheng Kaofu, humility, arrogance, Xu You, virtue, inner vision, nine tests of character</keywords>
